title: Elijah's Despair and the Quiet Sound
overview: Right after his triumph on Mount Carmel, Elijah flees a death threat, collapses in the desert, meets God at Mount Horeb (Sinai), and is sent back with new work and a successor.

parts.label: A death threat (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Elijah has just beaten Baal's prophets in a contest on Mount Carmel and had them killed, so Queen Jezebel, a foreign princess devoted to Baal, swears to kill him in return. He flees south to Beersheba, beyond King Ahab's kingdom; some translations say he was afraid, others that he 'saw' the danger, because the Hebrew can be read either way.

parts.label: Wanting to die (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Alone in the desert and worn out right after his greatest victory, Elijah asks God to take his life. Instead an angel twice wakes him with bread and water, and he walks forty days and nights to Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai, where God had met Moses.

parts.label: God passes by at Horeb (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: The LORD passes by, but is not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire; then comes a quiet sound, which translations render 'still small voice' or 'gentle whisper' and the Hebrew puts roughly as 'a sound of thin silence.' Many read this as God working without spectacle, unlike the fire on Carmel, yet Elijah's answer before and after is word for word the same: he alone is left.

parts.label: Three appointments (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: God sends Elijah back to anoint, meaning formally appoint, Hazael as king of Aram (Syria), Jehu as king of Israel, and Elisha as his own successor. God's reply to Elijah's complaint is grim: each will kill whoever escapes the one before, which 2 Kings later tells as war and bloody purges, though what Elisha's part in the killing means is unclear.

parts.label: Seven thousand faithful (v. 18)
parts.note: Elijah is not alone after all: God says seven thousand in Israel have never knelt to Baal or kissed his image, a gesture of worship. The number may be a round figure, and translations differ on whether God 'reserves' these people now or 'will leave' them as survivors of the coming judgment.

parts.label: Elisha's call (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: Elijah throws his cloak over Elisha, a farmer wealthy enough to plow with twelve pairs of oxen, to mark him as successor, and his odd reply to Elisha's wish to say goodbye may mean 'go, the choice is yours' or 'go, but remember what I just did.' Elisha then slaughters the oxen, cooks them on his burned plowing gear for the people and follows Elijah; many readers see this as a clean break with his old life, though the text does not say why he did it.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the chapter mainly shows Elijah failing and being corrected, even quietly replaced by Elisha, or a worn out servant being gently restored and sent back to work.
think: Elijah falls apart right after his biggest success; why do you think a high point can be followed so quickly by a low one?
